conclusions: Basic object/gripper geometry and opening information remain readable in RAW features on independent diagnostic groups.
Original-cache gripper position decoding worsens shallow4.53cm to deep5.13cm, then improves to fusion4.04cm; pre-pi4.04cm.
Controlled object decoding improves deep6.84cm to fusion5.96cm; relative-displacement decoding does not show a reliable fusion gain.
Fusion and pre-pi decoding are nearly identical. Current data do not identify fusion compression as a major information-loss point.
RAW gripper geometry decoding remains weaker than native RGB reference6.15cm vs3.45cm in controlled snapshots, with identical final-stage head capacity.
Additional post-fusion context contribution is mostly sample-invariant, and adds no clear decoding benefit in these targets; inspect this branch.
Fewshot256 does not materially improve held-out geometry readability under these fixed probes.
limits: Only small-head decodability measured; fixed8x8 pooling can hide information and failures do not prove absence.
Controlled snapshots can float/intersect objects and are a separate diagnostic distribution, not physical closed-loop rollouts.
Cached labels contain world EE positions and gripper-command proxies, not object positions; controlled data contain world TCP/object ground truth.
Probe test groups were not used for head training/selection, but frozen parent saw some cached source episodes.
Native RGB also has about5.2cm object probe error despite prior policy success; probe errors are not a closed-loop acceptance threshold.
No evidence here separates architecture from representation training adequacy or identifies sensor noise as the primary cause.
No hidden labels enter runtime policy inputs, no RGB teacher, no policy optimizer steps.
